name: Citric Acid
reasons: Naturally occurring organic acid commonly used to adjust acidity and enhance flavor.
Permitted by FSSAI and Codex Alimentarius under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) with no specific concern identified at typical usage levels.

name: Sodium Carbonates
reasons: Common leavening and raising agent used in baking (baking soda).
Permitted under Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP) by FSSAI.

name: Lecithins
reasons: Naturally derived phospholipid emulsifier commonly obtained from soy or sunflower.
Widely permitted by FSSAI to maintain emulsion stability in confectionery and baked goods.

name: Guar Gum
reasons: Plant-based hydrocolloid dietary fiber used to provide texture and viscosity.
Permitted food additive under FSSAI and international standards.

name: Xanthan Gum
reasons: Naturally fermented polysaccharide hydrocolloid produced by Xanthomonas campestris fermentation.
JECFA established an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 'not specified', confirming no specific food-safety concern under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP). Permitted widely by FSSAI and Codex.

name: Sodium Carboxymethyl Cellulose (CMC)
reasons: Purified soluble cellulose ether permitted under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) by Codex, JECFA (ADI 'not specified'), and FSSAI.
Functions as an indigestible dietary hydrocolloid providing texture and moisture retention without specific hazard at food-grade usage levels.

name: Silicon Dioxide
reasons: Inert mineral-derived anti-caking agent ensuring free flow of seasoning and powdered foods.
Permitted under standard food regulations (GMP limits).

name: Monosodium Glutamate (MSG)
reasons: Naturally derived or fermented sodium salt of glutamic acid used to impart umami (savory) taste.
JECFA and Codex Alimentarius evaluated MSG with an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 'not specified', indicating no specific concern identified at typical Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) levels.
Permitted by FSSAI with mandatory packaging label declaration ('Contains added MSG').

name: Caramel IV (Sulfite Ammonia Caramel)
reasons: Heat-treated carbohydrate coloring agent prepared with sulfite and ammonium compounds.
Permitted subject to maximum limits in soft drinks and confectionery by FSSAI.

name: Carrageenan
reasons: Naturally derived sulfated polygalactan extracted from red edible seaweeds, permitted under GMP by Codex, FSSAI, and FDA.

Some experimental animal and cellular models have studied gastrointestinal inflammatory pathways with degraded carrageenan (poligeenan); authoritative assessments (JECFA, EFSA) confirm food-grade (undegraded) carrageenan is safe at approved food-use levels.

name: Sucralose
reasons: Zero-calorie synthetic high-intensity sweetener derived by chlorination of sucrose.
Evaluated by JECFA, EFSA, and FDA with an established Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI 0-15 mg/kg bw). Permitted by FSSAI within maximum statutory limits.
Some experimental studies have examined gut microbiome interactions; scientific evidence at typical dietary exposure levels does not establish a confirmed food-safety hazard.

name: Polysorbate 80
reasons: Synthetic non-ionic surfactant and emulsifier permitted under specific statutory limits by Codex, FDA, and FSSAI.

JECFA established an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 0-25 mg/kg bw. In-vitro and rodent studies have explored mucosal interactions, while human clinical evaluations within permitted limits show acceptable tolerance.

name: Tartrazine
reasons: Synthetic azo dye providing bright lemon yellow coloration.
Permitted strictly within designated statutory limits (max 100 mg/kg) under FSSAI regulations.
Requires explicit color declaration on packaging due to sensitivities in susceptible individuals.

name: Sunset Yellow FCF
reasons: Synthetic petroleum-derived orange-yellow azo dye.
Subject to strict quantitative threshold limits under FSSAI food product regulations.

name: Sodium Benzoate
reasons: Antimicrobial chemical preservative active in acidic pH environments.
Permitted subject to statutory maximum levels (typically 120-750 ppm) under FSSAI.

name: Aspartame
reasons: Artificial non-caloric high-intensity sweetener.
Permitted with maximum allowable usage levels; requires statutory declaration 'CONTAINS PHENYLALANINE' for individuals with phenylketonuria (PKU).
Subject to Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI 0-40 mg/kg bw) evaluated by WHO/JECFA.

name: Butylated Hydroxyanisole (BHA)
reasons: Synthetic phenolic antioxidant permitted in edible oils and fats subject to statutory limits (typically 100-200 mg/kg).

JECFA established an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 0-0.5 mg/kg bw. High-dose rodent bioassays showed forestomach cellular proliferation, but human relevance at dietary levels remains controlled under strict regulatory caps.

name: Butylated Hydroxytoluene (BHT)
reasons: Synthetic lipophilic antioxidant used to inhibit oxidative rancidity in fats and oils.
Permitted under strict quantitative threshold limits by FSSAI and Codex. JECFA established an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) of 0-0.3 mg/kg bw.

name: Sodium Nitrite

jurisdictionalStatus.India: RESTRICTED (FSSAI limits residual levels in processed meat standards)
jurisdictionalStatus.European Union: RESTRICTED (Regulation (EC) No 1333/2008 sets strict maximum added limits)
jurisdictionalStatus.United States: RESTRICTED (FDA 21 CFR 172.175 limits to max 200 ppm in cured meats)

reasons: Inorganic salt used to prevent Clostridium botulinum spore outgrowth in processed meats.
Subject to stringent statutory maximum residual limits due to potential formation of nitrosamines under high heat.

name: Potassium Bromate

jurisdictionalStatus.United States: RESTRICTED (FDA recommends bakers avoid use; permitted under 21 CFR 136.110)

reasons: Regulatory Action (India): Statutorily prohibited by FSSAI and removed from the list of permitted food additives in 2016.
Scientific Evaluation (JECFA): Evaluated as a genotoxic carcinogen with conclusion that use as a flour treatment agent is not acceptable.
Codex Alimentarius: General Standard for Food Additives (CXS 192-1995) does not authorize potassium bromate for use in standardized flours.

name: Propylparaben

jurisdictionalStatus.United States: RESTRICTED (Prohibited in California under California Food Safety Act effective 2027; historical federal listing 21 CFR 184.1670)
jurisdictionalStatus.India: RESTRICTED (FSSAI standards do not permit propylparaben in general food categories)

reasons: Scientific Assessment (EFSA, 2004): Evaluated endocrine-disrupting potential and adverse reproductive effects in juvenile rodent models; concluded an Acceptable Daily Intake (ADI) could not be established.
Regulatory Action (European Union): Withdrawn from the list of authorized food additives in the EU pursuant to Commission Directive 2006/52/EC.
Regulatory Action (United States): Prohibited in food products under the California Food Safety Act (effective 2027); remains under federal FDA review.
Regulatory Action (India): FSSAI food product regulations do not include propylparaben in the general list of permitted preservatives.

name: Azodicarbonamide

jurisdictionalStatus.India: PROHIBITED (FSSAI Food Products Standards & Food Additives Regulations)
jurisdictionalStatus.Australia: PROHIBITED (FSANZ does not permit food additive use)
jurisdictionalStatus.United States: PERMITTED (FDA 21 CFR 172.806, max 45 ppm in flour)

reasons: Regulatory Status (India): Prohibited for use as a flour treatment agent under FSSAI regulations.
Regulatory Status (European Union & Australia): Prohibited for food use due to thermal degradation breakdown concerns.
Regulatory Status (United States): Permitted under FDA 21 CFR 172.806 as an aging and bleaching ingredient in cereal flour at levels not exceeding 45 ppm.
Scientific Evaluation (JECFA): Thermal decomposition during baking yields semicarbazide (SEM), which exhibited weak genotoxic potential in experimental models.

name: Titanium Dioxide

jurisdictionalStatus.India: RESTRICTED (FSSAI limits use to specified food categories)

reasons: Scientific Assessment (EFSA, 2021): Concluded titanium dioxide can no longer be considered safe as a food additive due to concerns regarding genotoxicity of nanoparticle fractions.
Regulatory Action (European Union): Banned as a food additive in the EU under Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/63.
Regulatory Action (United States): Permitted in food under FDA 21 CFR 73.575 up to 1% by weight pending ongoing re-evaluation.

name: Brominated Vegetable Oil
reasons: Regulatory Action (United States): FDA issued final rule revoking regulation authorizing BVO in food in 2024 following toxicological bioassays demonstrating tissue bioaccumulation and thyroid/hepatic toxicity.
Regulatory Action (India & European Union): Not authorized for use in food products under FSSAI and European Union regulations.

name: Red 3 (Erythrosine)

jurisdictionalStatus.United States: RESTRICTED (State prohibition in California from 2027; federal cosmetic ban)
jurisdictionalStatus.European Union: RESTRICTED (EFSA/Commission limits food use exclusively to cocktail/candied cherries)
jurisdictionalStatus.India: RESTRICTED (FSSAI permits within statutory limits, max 100 mg/kg in permitted foods)

reasons: Regulatory Status (United States): FDA banned cosmetic and externally applied uses; food use prohibited under California Food Safety Act (effective 2027).
Regulatory Status (European Union): Strictly restricted exclusively to cocktail cherries and candied cherries under EU regulations.
Regulatory Status (India): Permitted under FSSAI regulations strictly within statutory maximum limits (max 100 mg/kg) in specified product categories.
